title: Deuces Wild
full_review:
"Deuces Wild" (MGM) deals moviegoers a bad hand. In its artificial recreation of 1950s street gang wars, it is melodramatic and overdone, telling the most generic of stories without mustering up enough energy to sustain interest.

Stripping away any of the ethnic complexities found in the far superior "West Side Story" (a film "Deuces" attempts to imitate without the benefit of a great score or interesting story), director Scott Kalvert goes for a gritty, realistic feel that is never accomplished. If it weren't for the violence, the film could almost be considered campy as the director throws in one dramatic flair after another.

Deuces gang leader Leon (Stephen Dorff) has sworn to protect his Italian neighborhood from drugs after his brother Al died from a heroin overdose fed to him by Marco (Norman Reedus), the leader of the rival Viper gang. Three years later, the Dodgers have moved to Los Angeles and Marco is out of jail. The truce between the Deuces and Vipers ends, as Marco plans to set up a lucrative drug trade in the 'hood with the help of local gangster Fritzy (Matt Dillon).

In clumsy fashion, the film spells out that for the Deuces, loyalty is everything. So when Leon's brother Bobby (Brad Renfro) falls for the Annie (Fairuza Balk), the sister of Viper member Jimmy Pockets (Balthazar Getty), bonds are tested. But this romantic angle is strained, as if writers Paul Kimatian and Christopher Gambale knew this needed to be an ingredient in the script, but didn't know exactly what to do with it. The script itself seems stalled, as if scenes were poorly copied from other similar films as they went along.

Director Kalvert has staged the bloody fisticuffs -- powered by frenetic music -- in such a manner that it's hard to distinguish who's beating whom. Any realistic tone he tried to set is cancelled by the slow-motion camera work that draws way too much attention to itself. And despite the meticulous period costumes, cars, etc., the atmosphere feels phony, never transcending the trappings of a backstage lot. The age discrepancies of the actors and the characters they play are obvious. Leon is supposed to be a near manhood 18-year-old, but Dorff seems far older. On the other hand, Dillon seems too young to be a respected mafia man running the block.

The supporting cast is thrown away, with Deborah Harry hidden behind a ridiculous wig as Annie's loopy mother and Vincent Pastore as an ineffectual priest who advocates peace over violence.

An unimaginative display of silly macho posturing, "Deuces Wild" presents an overly familiar story without any fresh angles.

Due to much bloody violence, a sexual encounter, brief drug content and recurring rough language, the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops classification is A-IV -- adults, with reservations. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted. 2002
